sections.title: The one question
sections.body:
> At any moment we can answer: why can't this team send, who decided that, and what would change it?

Every table, column and feature earns its place by helping answer that question — for the **reviewer** looking at a case, the **customer** looking at their banner, or **us later** asking whether a detector is any good.

If it doesn't help answer it, it waits.

# Why this one
- It is what every complaint in the problem statement reduces to: reviewers can't see why, customers can't see why, re-enable doesn't say who or why, a wrong call leaves no trace.
- It names three audiences, so it pulls in the customer-facing work without making it the center.
- "What would change it" covers lifting, snoozing and allowances — the positive side — not just the restriction.

# Sign off if
You'd use this sentence to reject a feature in review.

sections.title: 1 · A restriction is a claim with a reason and a decider
sections.body:
A restriction says **what was found** and **who decided** to act on it.

- **Reason** — the kind of problem (a category such as `content.phishing`), and for an automation, the exact rule that fired.
- **Finding** — the specific thing found, when there is one: `email:<id>`, `word:crypto`.
- **Decider** — a **person** (by user id) or an **automation**, named with its version: `health-cron`, `phishtank-v0`, `ses`, `team-deletion`.

"Why can't this team send" is answered by the claims in effect, read straight off them.

# Scope: standing state
The question is about what **stays** blocked until something changes. A one-off rejection of a single send is answered on the spot in the error the customer sees, with its evidence logged — it is not a restriction.

# Rules in
- Decider separate from reason. A person who blocks must say why; there is no "admin judgment" reason.
- Recording a claim even when the domain is already off — otherwise the second reason is invisible.

# Rules out
- A free-text `disableCriterion` that only goes to logs.
- "detector" or "system" as an answer to who decided.

sections.title: 1b · Policies decide; restrictions record
sections.body:
A policy answers "given what we saw, should we act?". Enforcement answers "why can't this team send, who decided, what would change it?". They meet at one seam:

- **A policy changes sending state only by writing a restriction**, naming itself as the decider and a registered rule as the reason.
- **A policy reads allowances** as one of its inputs, and skips findings a person has allowed.
- **Enforcement never reads a policy.** Dependencies point one way: policies can be added, versioned or deleted without touching restrictions, lifts or allowances.

A policy's internal reasoning — the facts it cited, the model's answer — lives in its evidence, not in the restriction.

# Rules in
- safety-v0's `act` disabling a domain becomes "write a restriction".
- A future safety-log policy that blocks is one more caller of the same seam.

# Rules out
- A second override system next to allowances.
- Diagnostic outcomes (inconclusive, unsupported version) becoming restriction reasons.

sections.title: 2 · The remedy matches the finding
sections.body:
Act at the grain of what was found — and correct at the same grain.

| Finding is about | Restrict | Allow / correct |
|---|---|---|
| a word | (the domain, today) | that word, for that team |
| one email | that email (later), the domain today | that email |
| sending behavior | the domain | a quiet window on that reason |
| the account | the team | — |

# Rules in
- Team-scoped restrictions (provider pauses, suspicious signups, deletion are about the team).
- Approving one email lifts only that email's restriction — never a complaint-rate restriction or an admin block.
- Allowing a single banned word for a team, instead of exempting it from every check.

# Rules out
- Reenable clearing every flagged email the team ever sent.
- Unleash as the only way to loosen anything.

sections.title: 3 · A detector's verdict is provisional; a person's is binding
sections.body:
Machines may make claims. A person may **retract** one ("it was wrong") or **close** it ("they fixed it") — and that judgment holds until it expires. Detectors must respect it.

# Rules in
- A lift needs a person, a verdict (wrong / fixed) and a note.
- A "wrong" lift can leave an **allowance** behind, so the same finding doesn't restrict again the next time the detector runs.
- Allowances end on their own — a lapse moves toward safer, so no one has to act.

# Rules out
- A detector re-disabling a domain 15 minutes after a person lifted it for the same finding.
- SES reinstating a tenant counting as a lift (the provider is evidence, not a person).
- Permanent exemptions with no reason.

sections.title: 4 · Record what happened once; compute everything else
sections.body:
Claims and judgments are written once and never edited. A lift fills in empty fields exactly once; it never rewrites a claim.

"In effect", the review queue, "what's blocking re-enable" and the false-positive rate are **queries**, not stored state. The domain's `disabled` flag is a cache of "has a claim in effect".

# Rules in
- `liftedAt` / `revokedAt` written once, guarded by `WHERE liftedAt IS NULL` — a second lift, or one from a stale page, does nothing.
- "How often is this detector wrong" = count of claims lifted as wrong, by reason.

# Rules out
- Overwriting `decision` in place.
- `safetyClassification = "override"` replacing the classifier's label.

sections.title: 5 · Add a concept only when a real case needs it
sections.body:
A new concept enters only when a **real case** needs it **and** the existing concepts — restriction, lift, allowance — can't express it.

Before adding anything, write down the case and show why the three nouns can't cover it.

# What this rule removed from the earlier designs
- A generic decision log with seven kinds.
- Overturns of overturns; overturning evidence vs decision.
- Stale-decision version checks and "superseded" decisions.
- Idempotency keys (kept as a future change).
- Content-hash targets and policy replay — real eventually, not yet.

# Sign off if
You'd hold me to it the next time a design grows a new noun.

sections.title: Three nouns
sections.body:
```
Restriction
  teamId, sendingDomainId?          // null = the whole team
  category, ruleId?, findingKey?    // ruleId for an automation's claim
  deciderKind (person | automation), deciderName   // user id, or "health-cron@3"
  liftedAt?, liftedByUserId?, liftVerdict? (wrong | fixed), liftNote?   // written once

Allowance                            // exactly one selector
  teamId
  category + findingKey   |  ruleId  |  category  |  (none = all checks)
  until, grantedByUserId, note
  revokedAt?, revokedByUserId?      // written once
```

- **Disabled** = the domain or its team has a restriction with no `liftedAt`.
- **Dedupe** = an automation's repeat claim with the same rule + finding is skipped (under a row lock). A person's claim is never deduped against an automation's.
- **Automations** check allowances before restricting; a suppressed finding can be noted, not acted on.
- **The registry** (TS) holds categories and rules: subject, label, the finding type each rule produces.

No catch-all JSON. No generic event kinds.

sections.title: Reasons and how allowances match
sections.body:
**Category** — the kind of problem, stable: `content.phishing`, `content.banned_word`, `behavior.complaint_rate`, `behavior.provider_paused`, `account.suspicious_signup`, `account.deleted`, …

**Rule** — one automation's complete predicate, with an immutable id, in exactly one category: `phishing_classifier`, `classifier_unrecognized_output`, `banned_word_substring`, `lookalike_sender_root_plus_lure`, `health_complaint_limit`, … A rule whose meaning changes gets a new id.

**Finding** — typed and the same across rules: `email:<id>`, `word:<lowercased word>` (later `content:<hash>`).

# An allowance is one of three judgments
| A person says | Selector | Matches when |
|---|---|---|
| this finding was wrong | category + finding | same category and finding, any rule |
| this rule is wrong for this team | rule | same rule |
| this category is wrong for this team | category | same category |

Exact equality only — no prefixes, no precedence: any matching allowance suppresses.

- A finding allowance survives replacing the classifier with new rules; a rule allowance doesn't, and shouldn't.
- Editing the banned-word list doesn't touch word allowances.
- Creating an allowance doesn't lift what's already in effect; it governs what automations do next.
- A decision citing several rules writes one restriction per rule + finding; the review groups them by finding.

# Not reasons
Classifier `spam` / `safe` (accepted today), mail-smell (rejects creation — a one-off), Apple Private Relay notices (warnings), the volume/age gate (decides whether a claim restricts), facets (evidence until a rule uses them).

sections.title: How the original asks are met
sections.body:
| Ask | Met by |
|---|---|
| clear story of why it was disabled | reason + finding + actor on each restriction; the case page lists what's in effect |
| link disable and re-enable | the lift lives on the restriction it ends |
| mark a decision wrong without overwriting | the lift's verdict, written once |
| don't re-fire on what a person cleared | an allowance left by a "wrong" lift |
| allow a specific banned word for a team | an allowance: reason `banned_words`, finding `crypto` |
| review queue that tells the story | restrictions in effect, grouped by team, with reason and actor |

sections.title: Checked against earlier ideas
sections.body:
| Idea | Verdict | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| reason + decider | keep | 1 |
| decider = person or named automation | keep | 1 |
| finding key, typed across rules | keep | 2 |
| reason tree with prefix-matched allowances | drop (Codex) | 2, 5 |
| three exact allowance selectors | keep | 2, 3 |
| "admin judgment" as a reason | drop | 1 |
| team-scoped restrictions | keep | 2 |
| lift with wrong / fixed | keep | 3 |
| allowance (incl. banned word) | keep | 2, 3 |
| write-once lift fields | keep | 4 |
| generic decision log | drop | 5 |
| overturns of overturns | drop | 5 |
| version checks / superseded | drop | 5 |
| idempotency keys | later | 5 |
| snooze | when the queue needs it | 1 (what would change it) |
| content holds, policy replay | later | 5 |

sections.title: Phases
sections.body:
1. **Restrictions.** The table; every disable site writes one with reason, finding and actor; re-enable lifts them; the review page shows what's in effect; approving an email lifts only that email's restriction. Includes Codex's must-fixes: every enable goes through a lift, team scope, finding key.
2. **Lift with a verdict, and allowances.** The lift dialog (wrong / fixed + optional allowance); detectors check allowances; allow a word for a team.
3. **Notes and snooze.** When the review workflow needs them.
4. **One entry point for detectors** (`enforce`), with linked evidence.
5. **Customer surfaces** — banner, email, API error worded by subject.

sections.title: Open questions
sections.body:
- After a "wrong" lift, what is the **default allowance length** per reason?
- Is `DISABLE_SPAMMY_SENDING_DOMAINS` on in prod? (It re-disables on every cron run today.)
- After a team is **hard-deleted**, does its enforcement history survive (abuse record) or go (privacy)?
- How much do we tell customers about **content** flags?
